dosLagenReference: EN 301 549 V3.2.1, WCAG 2.1 Level AA required

remediation.description: Text and images of text must have a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 (3:1 for large text).
remediation.technicalGuidance: Use tools like WebAIM Contrast Checker to verify contrast. Adjust color choices or add background opacity to achieve correct contrast.

holmdigitalInsight.swedishInterpretation: One of the most common reasons for fines from regulators. Especially important for public sector monitoring.
commonMistakes: Gray text on white background (#777 on #FFF)
Placeholder text with too low contrast
holmdigitalInsight.diggPrecedent: Regulators often cite poor contrast in primary navigation elements.
holmdigitalInsight.priorityRationale: Critical for users with low vision. Affects readability for all users in varying lighting conditions.

legalContext.eaaAnnex: Annex I, Section I - Functional accessibility requirements

plainLanguage.headline: Button text is too faint against the background
plainLanguage.whatHappens: The text on buttons and links does not have enough contrast against the background for everyone to read it.
plainLanguage.whoIsAffected: Visitors with low vision, older users, and anyone visiting the site on a phone in bright sunlight.
plainLanguage.businessImpact: If your visitor cannot clearly read the most important button on the page, they will not click it. Weak contrast on key actions is costly.
plainLanguage.howToFix: Darken the text or lighten the background until the contrast is sufficient.

dosLagenReference: EN 301 549 V3.2.1, WCAG 2.1 Level A required

remediation.description: All functionality must be accessible via keyboard.
remediation.technicalGuidance: Use semantic HTML elements (button, a, input) instead of div/span with click handlers. Ensure tabindex is used correctly.

holmdigitalInsight.swedishInterpretation: Keyboard access is fundamental and non-negotiable. Top priority in compliance audits.
commonMistakes: Custom dropdown menus without keyboard support
Modal dialogs that trap focus incorrectly
holmdigitalInsight.diggPrecedent: Auditors have issued fines for sites where core functions (e.g. forms, navigation) are not keyboard accessible.
holmdigitalInsight.priorityRationale: Critical for users with motor disabilities and screen reader users.

legalContext.eaaAnnex: Annex I, Section I - Functional accessibility requirements

plainLanguage.headline: The site cannot be used without a mouse
plainLanguage.whatHappens: Parts of the site cannot be reached using only the keyboard, and there is no visible indication of where you are when moving through the page.
plainLanguage.whoIsAffected: People who do not use a mouse for various reasons, and anyone who prefers navigating by keyboard.
plainLanguage.businessImpact: If a menu or button cannot be reached by keyboard, that visitor is simply locked out.
plainLanguage.howToFix: Make sure everything clickable can be reached with the Tab key, and that focus is clearly visible at all times.

dosLagenReference: EN 301 549 V3.2.1, WCAG 2.1 Level A required

remediation.description: Images that convey information must have a text alternative that serves the equivalent purpose, while purely decorative images must be marked so assistive technology can ignore them. That marking is active: an empty alt (alt="") is the standard way, and leaving out the alt attribute entirely is not enough, because assistive technology then cannot ignore the image (a screen reader may, for example, read out the file name). The requirement is about the outcome, not the technique.
remediation.technicalGuidance: Add alt attributes to all img elements. For decorative images, use alt="". For informative images, concisely describe the content.

holmdigitalInsight.swedishInterpretation: Especially important for logos and informational graphics. Frequently checked in audits.
commonMistakes: Alt text that just says 'image' or 'icon'
holmdigitalInsight.diggPrecedent: Audits frequently cite missing alt text, especially for vital infographics.
holmdigitalInsight.priorityRationale: Critical for screen reader users to access visual information.

legalContext.eaaAnnex: Annex I, Section I - Functional accessibility requirements

plainLanguage.headline: Images have no description
plainLanguage.whatHappens: The images on the site have no text description in the code. A visitor using a screen reader hears only the word image, not what the image shows.
plainLanguage.whoIsAffected: Visitors with visual impairments, and also Google, which reads image descriptions to understand what your page is about.
plainLanguage.businessImpact: Images without descriptions become invisible to both screen readers and search engines. You lose visitors and search ranking at the same time.
plainLanguage.howToFix: Add a short description to each image that conveys information, for example Knitted wool sweater in grey. It takes a few seconds per image.

dosLagenReference: EN 301 549 V3.2.1, WCAG 2.1 Level A required

remediation.description: Form fields must have clear labels or instructions.
remediation.technicalGuidance: Use label elements linked to input via for/id. For complex forms, use fieldset and legend. Use aria-describedby for extra instructions.

holmdigitalInsight.swedishInterpretation: Forms are critical for e-services. Compliance is strictly enforced in public sector apps.
commonMistakes: Label and input not linked via for/id
holmdigitalInsight.diggPrecedent: Audit decisions often criticize poor form accessibility, especially for application and contact forms.
holmdigitalInsight.priorityRationale: Critical for users to successfully use e-services and submit information.

legalContext.eaaAnnex: Annex I, Section I - Functional accessibility requirements

plainLanguage.headline: Form fields are missing clear labels
plainLanguage.whatHappens: The input fields on the page have no connected label. A grey hint text may appear inside the field, but it disappears as soon as someone starts typing.
plainLanguage.whoIsAffected: Anyone using a screen reader, and visitors interrupted mid-form who lose track of where they were.
plainLanguage.businessImpact: Form fields without labels block visitors from completing key actions. Every barrier at critical forms costs you conversions.
plainLanguage.howToFix: Add a visible label above each field, for example Postcode, that stays visible at all times.

dosLagenReference: EN 301 549 V3.2.1, WCAG 2.1 Level A required

remediation.description: Each web page must have a descriptive title.
remediation.technicalGuidance: Use the title element in head. The title should be unique for each page and describe its purpose. Format: 'Page Name - Site Name'.

holmdigitalInsight.swedishInterpretation: Important for navigation, especially in SPAs where the title must update dynamically.
commonMistakes: Too long or too short title
holmdigitalInsight.diggPrecedent: Audits have noted missing page titles, especially in Single Page Applications.
holmdigitalInsight.priorityRationale: Important for screen reader navigation and SEO.

legalContext.eaaAnnex: Annex I, Section I - Functional accessibility requirements

plainLanguage.headline: The browser tab shows no clear page name
plainLanguage.whatHappens: The page has no descriptive title, or several pages share the same one. The title is the name shown in the browser tab, in bookmarks, and read aloud by a screen reader to say which page is open.
plainLanguage.whoIsAffected: Visitors using a screen reader, and anyone with many tabs open at once or looking for your page among their bookmarks.
plainLanguage.businessImpact: When every tab is named the same, or nothing at all, visitors cannot find their way back to your page among ten others. It becomes hard to bookmark and share, and you lose return visits.
plainLanguage.howToFix: Give each page its own descriptive title, for example Contact, Holm Digital. Your developer makes sure the title also updates when the content changes without the page reloading.

dosLagenReference: EN 301 549 V3.2.1, WCAG 2.1 Level A required

remediation.description: Information, structure, and relationships conveyed through presentation can be programmatically determined or are available in text.
remediation.technicalGuidance: Use semantic HTML: <header>, <nav>, <main>, <footer>, <h1>-<h6>, <ul>/ <ol>, <table>. Do not use visual styles to create 'fake' headings or lists.

holmdigitalInsight.swedishInterpretation: Semantic structure is crucial for screen readers to navigate effectively. Auditors often cite 'div-soup' that looks like structure but lacks semantics.
holmdigitalInsight.priorityRationale: Fundamental for all assistive technology navigation.

legalContext.eaaAnnex: Annex I, Section I - Functional accessibility requirements

plainLanguage.headline: The page structure is only skin deep
plainLanguage.whatHappens: What looks like headings and lists is really just text made large or bold. In the code there is no real structure, so assistive technology cannot tell what belongs together.
plainLanguage.whoIsAffected: Visitors using a screen reader, who listen their way through the page and rely on structure to tell what is a heading, what is a list, and what belongs together.
plainLanguage.businessImpact: A screen reader reads everything out as one grey blur. The visitor cannot get to what they came for and leaves.
plainLanguage.howToFix: Your developer builds headings, lists, and tables with the right code instead of just making text large or bold. Then assistive technology understands the structure.

dosLagenReference: EN 301 549 V3.2.1, WCAG 2.1 Level A required

remediation.description: Color is not used as the only visual means of conveying information, indicating an action, prompting a response, or distinguishing a visual element.
remediation.technicalGuidance: Complement color with text, icons, or underlining. E.g. links must have underlines or another visual marker besides color. Error messages need text/icon, not just a red border.

holmdigitalInsight.swedishInterpretation: Common problem in graphs and maps where only color coding is used.
commonMistakes: Links that only differ by color from body text
Error messages only marked with red color
Graphs where only color distinguishes data points

legalContext.eaaAnnex: Annex I, Section I - Functional accessibility requirements

plainLanguage.headline: Important information is shown by colour alone
plainLanguage.whatHappens: The page uses colour as the only way to convey something, for example a red border to mark an error, or colour as the only difference between a link and plain text. If you cannot see the colour, you miss the information.
plainLanguage.whoIsAffected: People with colour blindness or reduced colour vision (around one man in twelve), people with low vision, and anyone reading the page in bright sunlight or in greyscale.
plainLanguage.businessImpact: If a visitor does not notice that a field is filled in wrong, or does not see that a piece of text is a clickable link, they get stuck. What was meant to guide them becomes a dead end.
plainLanguage.howToFix: Always back up colour with something more, for example a text, an icon, or an underline. Your developer marks links and error messages so they show even without colour.

dosLagenReference: EN 301 549 V3.2.1, WCAG 2.1 Level AA required

remediation.description: Content must be presentable without requiring scrolling in two dimensions down to 320px width.
remediation.technicalGuidance: Use responsive design (CSS Media Queries, Flexbox, Grid). Avoid fixed widths in pixels. Ensure tables and images scale correctly.

holmdigitalInsight.swedishInterpretation: A modern requirement (WCAG 2.1) critical for mobile use and magnified text. DIGG has zero tolerance for horizontal scroll on vertical sites.
holmdigitalInsight.priorityRationale: Critical for low vision users who zoom in heavily.

legalContext.eaaAnnex: Annex I, Section I - Functional accessibility requirements

plainLanguage.headline: The page breaks out of its frame when you zoom in
plainLanguage.whatHappens: When a visitor enlarges the page or uses a narrow screen, the content does not fit, and they are forced to scroll sideways to read every line.
plainLanguage.whoIsAffected: People with low vision who enlarge the text a lot, and anyone visiting the site on a phone.
plainLanguage.businessImpact: Scrolling back and forth on every line is such hard work that most give up. You lose mobile visitors in particular, who are often the majority.
plainLanguage.howToFix: Your developer makes sure the content reflows and adapts to the width of the screen instead of staying fixed in a wide layout.

dosLagenReference: EN 301 549 V3.2.1, WCAG 2.1 Level AA required

remediation.description: The visual presentation of user interface components and graphical objects must have a contrast ratio of at least 3:1 against adjacent colors.
remediation.technicalGuidance: Applies to buttons, input borders, icons, and focus indicators. Ensure all interactive elements are clearly visible against the background.

holmdigitalInsight.swedishInterpretation: Often missed requirement regarding focus rings and inactive (but visible) components. Important for understanding the interface.
commonMistakes: Grayed out buttons with too low contrast

legalContext.eaaAnnex: Annex I, Section I - Functional accessibility requirements

plainLanguage.headline: Buttons and fields barely show against the background
plainLanguage.whatHappens: The edges of buttons, fields, and icons have too little contrast against the background. It is not clear where to click or type.
plainLanguage.whoIsAffected: People with low vision, older users, and anyone in bright light or on a cheap screen.
plainLanguage.businessImpact: If a visitor cannot see that something is clickable, they do not use it. An invisible button is an unused button.
plainLanguage.howToFix: Your developer makes the edges of buttons, fields, and key icons clearer against the background so people can see where to press.

dosLagenReference: EN 301 549 V3.2.1, WCAG 2.1 Level AA required

remediation.description: Content or functionality must not be lost when the user changes text spacing (line height, paragraph spacing, etc.).
remediation.technicalGuidance: Avoid fixed heights on text containers. Let containers grow with content. Test with text spacing bookmarklet.

holmdigitalInsight.swedishInterpretation: Important for dyslexia adaptations.
commonMistakes: Text container that does not grow

legalContext.eaaAnnex: Annex I, Section I - Functional accessibility requirements

plainLanguage.headline: Text gets cut off when you space it out
plainLanguage.whatHappens: Some visitors increase the space between lines and letters so they can read. When they do, text spills out of its box or gets cut off, and content disappears.
plainLanguage.whoIsAffected: People with dyslexia or low vision who set wider spacing to make reading manageable.
plainLanguage.businessImpact: If the text breaks the moment a visitor adjusts it, they cannot read it, and a reader who cannot read does not buy.
plainLanguage.howToFix: Your developer lets the boxes grow with the text instead of using fixed heights, so nothing is cut off.

dosLagenReference: EN 301 549 V3.2.1, WCAG 2.1 Level AA required

remediation.description: Content shown on hover/focus (e.g. tooltips) must be Dismissable, Hoverable, and Persistent.
remediation.technicalGuidance: Ensure tooltips do not disappear when moving mouse from trigger to the tooltip itself. Allow ESC to dismiss.

holmdigitalInsight.swedishInterpretation: Common problem with custom tooltips and mega-menus.
commonMistakes: Tooltips that cannot be reached with mouse
Content that cannot be dismissed without moving focus
holmdigitalInsight.priorityRationale: Important for users with magnification and motor difficulties.

legalContext.eaaAnnex: Annex I, Section I - Functional accessibility requirements

plainLanguage.headline: Small help boxes vanish before you can read them
plainLanguage.whatHappens: Text that appears when you move the pointer over something, for example a small explanation box, disappears as soon as you move the pointer, or cannot be closed.
plainLanguage.whoIsAffected: People who magnify the screen and have to move the pointer to read, and people with motor difficulties who struggle to hold the pointer still.
plainLanguage.businessImpact: If the help text vanishes before the visitor has read it, the help never lands, and a confused visitor gives up.
plainLanguage.howToFix: Your developer makes sure these boxes stay put until you are done, can be read with the pointer on them, and can be dismissed.

dosLagenReference: EN 301 549 V3.2.1, WCAG 2.1 Level A required

remediation.description: Captions must be provided for all prerecorded audio content in synchronized media.
remediation.technicalGuidance: Use the <track> element with WebVTT files for HTML5 video. For social media embeds, ensure captions are enabled.

holmdigitalInsight.swedishInterpretation: One of the most common deficiencies in the public sector. The legal requirement is strict: video with audio MUST have captions.
commonMistakes: Auto-generated captions that satisfy no one
Captions burned into video (not accessible for search/translation)
holmdigitalInsight.priorityRationale: Critical for deaf and hard of hearing users.

legalContext.eaaAnnex: Annex I, Section I - Functional accessibility requirements

plainLanguage.headline: The videos have no captions
plainLanguage.whatHappens: Video with speech has no captions, so everything said can only be taken in through the sound.
plainLanguage.whoIsAffected: People who are deaf or hard of hearing, but also anyone watching with the sound off in a quiet place or on a noisy bus.
plainLanguage.businessImpact: Without captions the whole message of the video is lost for a large group. Content they cannot take in does not sell.
plainLanguage.howToFix: Add accurate captions to every video with speech. Auto generated captions always need to be checked and corrected.

dosLagenReference: EN 301 549 V3.2.1, WCAG 2.1 Level AA required

remediation.description: Audio description must be provided for all prerecorded video content.
remediation.technicalGuidance: Either as a separate audio track, an alternative version of the video, or (if 'talking heads') ensuring all info is conveyed by audio.

holmdigitalInsight.swedishInterpretation: Can often be solved by 'integrated description' (talking about what is seen), which is more cost-effective.
commonMistakes: Information shown only visually (graphics, text signs) without being mentioned in audio

legalContext.eaaAnnex: Annex I, Section I - Functional accessibility requirements

plainLanguage.headline: The video does not tell you what only appears on screen
plainLanguage.whatHappens: In the video, important information is shown only on screen, for example text or something happening, without being said in the audio.
plainLanguage.whoIsAffected: People who cannot see the screen and have only the sound to go on.
plainLanguage.businessImpact: Someone who listens but cannot see misses part of the message and gets half the story. The point of the video is lost for them.
plainLanguage.howToFix: Make sure everything important shown on screen is also said in the audio, either in the narration or in a version with audio description.

dosLagenReference: EN 301 549 V3.2.1, WCAG 2.1 Level AA required

remediation.description: Content must not restrict its view and operation to a single display orientation, unless a specific orientation is essential.
remediation.technicalGuidance: Do not lock screen to portrait or landscape via CSS or JS manifest. Use CSS media queries to handle layout changes.

holmdigitalInsight.swedishInterpretation: Important for tablets and users who have the device mounted (e.g., wheelchair).
commonMistakes: Apps/sites that rotate interface 90 degrees against user will
holmdigitalInsight.priorityRationale: Important for users who cannot rotate their device.

legalContext.eaaAnnex: Annex I, Section I - Functional accessibility requirements

plainLanguage.headline: The page locks to portrait or landscape
plainLanguage.whatHappens: The site forces one orientation, portrait or landscape, and cannot be turned the way the visitor wants.
plainLanguage.whoIsAffected: People whose tablet or phone is fixed in place, for example on a wheelchair, and who cannot turn the device themselves.
plainLanguage.businessImpact: Anyone who cannot turn their device is shut out completely. For them the site is unusable even if everything else works.
plainLanguage.howToFix: Your developer removes the lock so the page works both in portrait and landscape.

dosLagenReference: EN 301 549 V3.2.1, WCAG 2.1 Level AA required

remediation.description: The purpose of each input field collecting information about the user can be programmatically determined.
remediation.technicalGuidance: Use the 'autocomplete' attribute on input fields for personal data (name, email, tel, address etc.).

holmdigitalInsight.swedishInterpretation: Makes it much easier to fill confusing forms (autofill).
holmdigitalInsight.priorityRationale: Reduces cognitive load and motor requirements.

legalContext.eaaAnnex: Annex I, Section I - Functional accessibility requirements

plainLanguage.headline: The form does not help fill itself in
plainLanguage.whatHappens: The fields for name, address, and the like are not marked with what they hold, so the browser cannot fill them in for the visitor automatically.
plainLanguage.whoIsAffected: People with motor difficulties or a cognitive disability, who are spared a lot of typing when details are filled in automatically.
plainLanguage.businessImpact: The more a visitor has to type by hand, the more drop out partway. Automatic filling means more of them finish.
plainLanguage.howToFix: Your developer marks up the fields so the browser's saved details can be filled in with one click.

dosLagenReference: EN 301 549 V3.2.1, WCAG 2.1 Level A required

remediation.description: If focus can be moved to a component of the page using a keyboard interface, then focus can be moved away from that component using only a keyboard interface.
remediation.technicalGuidance: Be careful with JS widgets that trap focus (e.g. modal windows). Ensure there is always a way out (e.g. ESC or shift+tab).

holmdigitalInsight.swedishInterpretation: A keyboard trap is a 'blocker' that makes the website unusable. Serious error.
commonMistakes: Custom widgets that loop focus infinitely
Embedded third-party components (maps, chats) without exit
holmdigitalInsight.priorityRationale: Critical: The user gets stuck and must restart the browser.

legalContext.eaaAnnex: Annex I, Section I - Functional accessibility requirements

plainLanguage.headline: Visitors get stuck and cannot move on
plainLanguage.whatHappens: Part of the page captures the keyboard so visitors can get in but not back out. It often happens in pop-ups, maps, or chat windows that offer no way out.
plainLanguage.whoIsAffected: People who use a keyboard or screen reader instead of a mouse, and anyone who cannot point and click for motor reasons.
plainLanguage.businessImpact: Once a visitor is caught in a trap, the whole page is closed to them, often the only way out is to shut the browser and start over. If the trap is in the checkout or a form, the sale is lost on the spot.
plainLanguage.howToFix: Your developer makes sure the keyboard can always leave every part of the page, for example with Esc or by tabbing onward. Check your own pop-ups and anything embedded from other services in particular, such as a chat or a map.

dosLagenReference: EN 301 549 V3.2.1, WCAG 2.1 Level A required

remediation.description: If a keyboard shortcut consists of only one character (letter, number, symbol), there must be a way to turn it off or remap it, or it must only be active on focus.
remediation.technicalGuidance: Avoid single-key shortcuts if possible. If needed, ensure they do not conflict with voice control or accidental typing.

holmdigitalInsight.swedishInterpretation: Important for voice control users (Dragon etc.) where single words can trigger commands accidentally.
commonMistakes: Gmail-like shortcuts that are on by default without option to disable

legalContext.eaaAnnex: Annex I, Section I - Functional accessibility requirements

plainLanguage.headline: Single key presses trigger things by accident
plainLanguage.whatHappens: The site has shortcuts that react to a single key. A mistaken press, or even speaking, is enough to make something happen unintentionally.
plainLanguage.whoIsAffected: People who control the computer by voice, where a single spoken word can happen to trigger a shortcut.
plainLanguage.businessImpact: Accidental commands cause confusion and mistakes, but they affect a small group and can often be avoided.
plainLanguage.howToFix: Your developer lets the visitor turn off or change the shortcuts, or makes sure they only apply when the right part of the page is in focus.

dosLagenReference: EN 301 549 V3.2.1, WCAG 2.1 Level A required

remediation.description: If a time limit (session, reading time) is set, the user must be able to turn off, adjust, or extend it.
remediation.technicalGuidance: Provide a warning before the session expires with an 'Extend session' button. The time limit must be at least 20 seconds.

holmdigitalInsight.swedishInterpretation: Critical for e-services/banking. Users who read slowly or use assistive technology need more time.
commonMistakes: Time limits that cannot be extended
holmdigitalInsight.priorityRationale: Critical to avoid losing entered data.

legalContext.eaaAnnex: Annex I, Section I - Functional accessibility requirements

plainLanguage.headline: You get logged out before you can finish
plainLanguage.whatHappens: The page has a time limit that runs out without warning. If you have not filled things in fast enough, you are logged out and what you entered is gone.
plainLanguage.whoIsAffected: People who read or type slowly, use assistive technology, or need more time for any reason at all.
plainLanguage.businessImpact: Losing everything you entered partway through an application or a purchase is so frustrating that many never come back. That is where the sale dies.
plainLanguage.howToFix: Warn before the time runs out and give a clear button to extend it. Let the visitor have more time instead of throwing them out.

dosLagenReference: EN 301 549 V3.2.1, WCAG 2.1 Level A required

remediation.description: For moving, blinking, or scrolling content that starts automatically and lasts more than 5 seconds, there must be a way to pause, stop, or hide it.
remediation.technicalGuidance: Applies to carousels (sliders), auto-updating news feeds, animated backgrounds. Add a clear pause button.

holmdigitalInsight.swedishInterpretation: Important for users with concentration difficulties (ADHD/Autism) who are distracted by movement.
commonMistakes: Animated backgrounds that cannot be turned off

legalContext.eaaAnnex: Annex I, Section I - Functional accessibility requirements

plainLanguage.headline: Moving content cannot be stopped
plainLanguage.whatHappens: Something on the page moves, blinks, or changes on its own and cannot be paused.
plainLanguage.whoIsAffected: People with concentration difficulties, for example ADHD, and people who read slowly and do not finish before the image changes.
plainLanguage.businessImpact: Constant movement pulls the eye away from what matters. The visitor loses focus on your message and on the buy button.
plainLanguage.howToFix: Your developer adds a clear pause button to slideshows and anything else that moves on its own.

dosLagenReference: EN 301 549 V3.2.1, WCAG 2.1 Level A required

remediation.description: Content must not flash more than three times per second (can cause seizures).
remediation.technicalGuidance: Avoid rapid flashing in video and animations. Use tools to measure flash frequency (PEAT).

holmdigitalInsight.swedishInterpretation: Health risk. Zero tolerance.

legalContext.eaaAnnex: Annex I, Section I - Functional accessibility requirements

plainLanguage.headline: Flashing content can trigger epileptic seizures
plainLanguage.whatHappens: Something on the page flashes quickly, more than three times a second. Flashing like this can bring on seizures.
plainLanguage.whoIsAffected: People with photosensitive epilepsy, for whom rapid flashing is a direct health risk.
plainLanguage.businessImpact: This is a safety matter, not just a comfort. A visitor who is risking their health leaves the site at once, and you risk your reputation.
plainLanguage.howToFix: Remove or slow down anything that flashes quickly so nothing flashes more than three times a second.

dosLagenReference: EN 301 549 V3.2.1, WCAG 2.1 Level A required

remediation.description: There must be a way to skip blocks of content that are repeated on multiple pages (e.g. navigation).
remediation.technicalGuidance: Implement a 'Skip to Main Content' link at the top of the page that becomes visible on focus. Use semantic landmarks (<main>, <nav>).

holmdigitalInsight.swedishInterpretation: Standard on all public sector sites. Enormously helpful for keyboard users.
commonMistakes: Skip-link broken (does not move focus correctly)

legalContext.eaaAnnex: Annex I, Section I - Functional accessibility requirements

plainLanguage.headline: Visitors are dragged through the whole menu on every page
plainLanguage.whatHappens: There is no way to skip past the menu and go straight to the content. Anyone navigating by keyboard has to step through every menu link on each new page.
plainLanguage.whoIsAffected: People who navigate by keyboard or screen reader instead of a mouse.
plainLanguage.businessImpact: Wearing the visitor down with the same menu clicks over and over makes them give up before they reach what matters.
plainLanguage.howToFix: Your developer adds a skip to content link at the very top that becomes visible when you tab to it.

dosLagenReference: EN 301 549 V3.2.1, WCAG 2.1 Level A required

remediation.description: Focus order must be logical and follow meaning/structure.
remediation.technicalGuidance: Match DOM order with visual order. Avoid tabindex greater than 0. Manage focus manually in modals and menus.

holmdigitalInsight.swedishInterpretation: Critical for complex layouts (Grid/Flexbox) where visual order may differ from DOM order.
commonMistakes: Modal closes and focus returns to top of page
holmdigitalInsight.priorityRationale: Critical for keyboard navigation and understanding.

legalContext.eaaAnnex: Annex I, Section I - Functional accessibility requirements

plainLanguage.headline: The keyboard jumps around the page at random
plainLanguage.whatHappens: When you move through the page with the keyboard, the highlight jumps in an illogical order, not the order the content appears on screen.
plainLanguage.whoIsAffected: People who navigate by keyboard or screen reader and rely on the order following what they see.
plainLanguage.businessImpact: Unpredictable jumping makes the page confusing to use. The visitor loses the thread and quits.
plainLanguage.howToFix: Your developer makes sure the highlight follows the same order the content appears in on screen.

dosLagenReference: EN 301 549 V3.2.1, WCAG 2.1 Level A required

remediation.description: The purpose of each link can be understood from the link text alone or from the link text together with its context.
remediation.technicalGuidance: Avoid 'Read more' or 'Click here'. Write descriptive link texts. Use aria-label if visual space is limited but more info is needed.

holmdigitalInsight.swedishInterpretation: Important for users navigating via link lists (screen readers).
commonMistakes: Links that don't say where they lead

legalContext.eaaAnnex: Annex I, Section I - Functional accessibility requirements

plainLanguage.headline: Links that only say read more
plainLanguage.whatHappens: Several links have no descriptive text and just say read more or click here.
plainLanguage.whoIsAffected: Anyone navigating by links using a keyboard or screen reader gets a list of read more, read more, read more without knowing where they lead.
plainLanguage.businessImpact: Confused visitors do not click. Search engines also favour links that describe what they lead to.
plainLanguage.howToFix: Replace read more with what the link actually leads to, for example Read our accessibility statement.

dosLagenReference: EN 301 549 V3.2.1, WCAG 2.1 Level AA required

remediation.description: There must be more than one way to find a web page within a set of web pages.
remediation.technicalGuidance: At least two of: Menu, Search, Sitemap, Links in content.

holmdigitalInsight.swedishInterpretation: Often fulfilled by menu + search. Sitemap is best practice.
commonMistakes: Missing search on sites with many pages

legalContext.eaaAnnex: Annex I, Section I - Functional accessibility requirements

plainLanguage.headline: There is only one way to find things on the site
plainLanguage.whatHappens: The visitor can only get around one single way, for example through the menu, with no search function or table of contents as an alternative.
plainLanguage.whoIsAffected: People who find menus hard to navigate and would rather search, and anyone looking for a specific page on a large site.
plainLanguage.businessImpact: If a visitor cannot find their way, they do not find it at all. An extra way to navigate catches more of them.
plainLanguage.howToFix: Offer at least two ways to find things, for example both a menu and a search function.

dosLagenReference: EN 301 549 V3.2.1, WCAG 2.1 Level AA required

remediation.description: Headings and labels must describe topic or purpose.
remediation.technicalGuidance: Write clear, descriptive headings that give meaning to the content below them. Form labels must be understandable.

holmdigitalInsight.swedishInterpretation: About editorial quality and comprehensibility.
commonMistakes: Labels that don't match what needs to be filled in

legalContext.eaaAnnex: Annex I, Section I - Functional accessibility requirements

plainLanguage.headline: Headings and field names do not say what they are about
plainLanguage.whatHappens: The headings and the names of form fields are vague or cryptic and do not describe what comes under them or what to fill in.
plainLanguage.whoIsAffected: All visitors, but especially those who skim by headings with a screen reader and rely on them to know where to go.
plainLanguage.businessImpact: Unclear headings mean the visitor does not find the right place and guesses wrong. Clear headings lead faster to the goal and to a purchase.
plainLanguage.howToFix: Write headings and field names that say exactly what they are about, for example Delivery address instead of Step 2.

dosLagenReference: EN 301 549 V3.2.1, WCAG 2.1 Level AA required

remediation.description: Any user interface operable by keyboard must have a visible focus indicator.
remediation.technicalGuidance: Never remove outline with CSS (outline: none) without replacing it with a clear visual indicator. Ensure contrast of focus ring is sufficient (see 1.4.11).

holmdigitalInsight.swedishInterpretation: One of the most common errors. Often because designers dislike the 'blue ring'.
holmdigitalInsight.priorityRationale: Critical: Without visible focus, the keyboard user doesn't know where they are.

legalContext.eaaAnnex: Annex I, Section I - Functional accessibility requirements

plainLanguage.headline: You cannot see which button or link the visitor has selected
plainLanguage.whatHappens: When the visitor moves around the page with the keyboard, there is no sign of which button or link is selected right now. The highlight that should show where focus sits is removed or too faint.
plainLanguage.whoIsAffected: People who navigate by keyboard instead of a mouse, whether for motor reasons or habit, and anyone temporarily without a working mouse.
plainLanguage.businessImpact: If visitors cannot see where they are on the page, clicking the right thing becomes a guessing game. Many give up partway through a form or a purchase, because no one wants to press blind.
plainLanguage.howToFix: Never remove the highlight that shows focus. Your developer makes sure the selected button or link gets a clear outline with enough contrast.

dosLagenReference: EN 301 549 V3.2.1, WCAG 2.1 Level A required

remediation.description: The default human language of each web page must be programmatically determinable.
remediation.technicalGuidance: Set the 'lang' attribute on the <html> element. E.g., <html lang='en'> for English.

holmdigitalInsight.swedishInterpretation: Fundamental for screen reading. Without this, the screen reader guesses the language, often leading to wrong pronunciation.
commonMistakes: Wrong language code (e.g. 'en' on a Swedish page)

legalContext.eaaAnnex: Annex I, Section I - Functional accessibility requirements

plainLanguage.headline: The page does not declare its language
plainLanguage.whatHappens: The code does not specify what language the page is written in.
plainLanguage.whoIsAffected: A screen reader then reads the text using the wrong pronunciation, which becomes incomprehensible.
plainLanguage.businessImpact: Your customer cannot understand what is read aloud and gives up.
plainLanguage.howToFix: Add a single line to the code that declares the language. One line, and it applies to the whole site.

dosLagenReference: EN 301 549 V3.2.1, WCAG 2.1 Level AA required

remediation.description: The human language of each passage or phrase in the content must be programmatically determinable.
remediation.technicalGuidance: Use the lang attribute on elements that differ from the page's main language. E.g. Bonjour.

holmdigitalInsight.swedishInterpretation: Rarely a critical error unless it significantly hinders understanding.
commonMistakes: Foreign quotes in text without markup

legalContext.eaaAnnex: Annex I, Section I - Functional accessibility requirements

plainLanguage.headline: Foreign words are read out with the wrong pronunciation
plainLanguage.whatHappens: Single words or quotes in another language are not marked in the code. The screen reader reads them with the wrong pronunciation and they come out as gibberish.
plainLanguage.whoIsAffected: People using a screen reader who come across a phrase in another language in the middle of the main text.
plainLanguage.businessImpact: The odd misreading is annoying but rarely sinks the whole experience. It is mostly a matter of finish.
plainLanguage.howToFix: Your developer marks up the foreign words with the right language so they are pronounced correctly.

dosLagenReference: EN 301 549 V3.2.1, WCAG 2.1 Level A required

remediation.description: When a component receives focus, it must not initiate a change of context.
remediation.technicalGuidance: Do not open new windows, submit forms, or move focus automatically just because user tabs to a field.

holmdigitalInsight.swedishInterpretation: Very confusing for users. Creates a feeling of lack of control.
commonMistakes: Dropdowns that navigate immediately upon selection (without 'Go' button)
Forms that auto-submit on last field focus

legalContext.eaaAnnex: Annex I, Section I - Functional accessibility requirements

plainLanguage.headline: Things happen just because you reach a field
plainLanguage.whatHappens: The moment a field or menu receives the highlight, something unexpected happens, for example a new window opens or the page changes.
plainLanguage.whoIsAffected: People who navigate by keyboard or screen reader and only wanted to move to the field, not start anything.
plainLanguage.businessImpact: Unexpected jumps make the visitor feel they are losing control. An uneasy visitor does not dare to carry on.
plainLanguage.howToFix: Your developer makes sure nothing starts just because you move to a field. Something should only happen when the visitor chooses it themselves.

dosLagenReference: EN 301 549 V3.2.1, WCAG 2.1 Level A required

remediation.description: Changing the setting of any component does not automatically cause a change of context unless the user has been advised of the behavior before using the component.
remediation.technicalGuidance: Inform the user that selection in a list reloads the page. Preferably, add a button to confirm the choice.

holmdigitalInsight.swedishInterpretation: Common in filtering functions.

legalContext.eaaAnnex: Annex I, Section I - Functional accessibility requirements

plainLanguage.headline: The page reloads as soon as you make a choice
plainLanguage.whatHappens: When the visitor picks something from a list or ticks a box, the page reloads or moves, without warning.
plainLanguage.whoIsAffected: People using a screen reader and people with a cognitive disability, who lose their place when the page suddenly changes.
plainLanguage.businessImpact: Unpredictable reloads in the middle of a choice make the visitor uneasy and they quit.
plainLanguage.howToFix: Your developer lets the visitor finish their choices and confirm with a button, instead of the page changing at every click.

dosLagenReference: EN 301 549 V3.2.1, WCAG 2.1 Level AA required

remediation.description: Navigational mechanisms that are repeated on multiple Web pages occur in the same relative order each time they are repeated.
remediation.technicalGuidance: Main menu should look the same and be in the same place on all pages. Search function as well.

holmdigitalInsight.swedishInterpretation: Predictability is key to cognitive accessibility.
commonMistakes: Menus that change place or order on different pages

legalContext.eaaAnnex: Annex I, Section I - Functional accessibility requirements

plainLanguage.headline: The menu moves around between pages
plainLanguage.whatHappens: The menu and other recurring parts sit in different places or in a different order on different pages.
plainLanguage.whoIsAffected: People with a cognitive disability and anyone who has learned where things are and then cannot find them again.
plainLanguage.businessImpact: If the visitor has to hunt for the menu afresh on every page, they tire of it. Recognition makes the site faster to use.
plainLanguage.howToFix: Keep the menu and recurring elements in the same place and the same order on every page.

dosLagenReference: EN 301 549 V3.2.1, WCAG 2.1 Level AA required

remediation.description: Components that have the same functionality within a set of Web pages are identified consistently.
remediation.technicalGuidance: Don't call search 'Search' on one page and 'Find' on another. Use the same icon for the same function.

holmdigitalInsight.swedishInterpretation: Important for usability.

legalContext.eaaAnnex: Annex I, Section I - Functional accessibility requirements

plainLanguage.headline: The same function is named differently in different places
plainLanguage.whatHappens: One and the same function is called different things or shown with different icons on different pages, for example Search in one place and Find in another.
plainLanguage.whoIsAffected: People with a cognitive disability and anyone who recognises a button by its name or icon.
plainLanguage.businessImpact: Different names for the same thing make the visitor think they are different functions. That creates hesitation and needless support questions.
plainLanguage.howToFix: Use the same name and the same icon for the same function everywhere on the site.

dosLagenReference: EN 301 549 V3.2.1, WCAG 2.1 Level A required

remediation.description: If an input error is automatically detected, the item that is in error is identified and the error is described to the user in text.
remediation.technicalGuidance: Show error message close to the field. Link with aria-describedby or include in label. Do not just color the field red.

holmdigitalInsight.swedishInterpretation: Critical for completing tasks. Generic error messages ('Something went wrong') are not accepted if the error is specific.
commonMistakes: Error message not visible to screen readers

legalContext.eaaAnnex: Annex I, Section I - Functional accessibility requirements

plainLanguage.headline: The form does not say what went wrong
plainLanguage.whatHappens: When the visitor fills in something wrong in a form, the error is not explained in text, or the field is only marked with a colour. It does not say which field is wrong or how to fix it.
plainLanguage.whoIsAffected: Visitors using a screen reader who cannot see a red mark, people with low vision, and anyone rushing through a form who needs clear guidance.
plainLanguage.businessImpact: A form that does not say what went wrong makes the visitor try again and again and finally give up. Every abandoned form is a lost contact, booking, or order.
plainLanguage.howToFix: Your developer shows a clear error message in text near the field, pointing out exactly what is wrong and how to fix it. Something went wrong is not enough when the error is known.

dosLagenReference: EN 301 549 V3.2.1, WCAG 2.1 Level AA required

remediation.description: If an input error is automatically detected and suggestions for correction are known, then the suggestions are provided to the user.
remediation.technicalGuidance: If date format is wrong, show required format (YYYY-MM-DD). Offer spelling suggestions for search ('Did you mean...?').

holmdigitalInsight.swedishInterpretation: About being helpful. Reduces support cases.
commonMistakes: Only saying 'Error' without saying how to fix it

legalContext.eaaAnnex: Annex I, Section I - Functional accessibility requirements

plainLanguage.headline: The error message does not say how to fix it
plainLanguage.whatHappens: When a visitor fills in something incorrectly, the page only says it is wrong, without explaining what is expected or how to correct it.
plainLanguage.whoIsAffected: Anyone filling in a form, especially those who cannot easily guess the right format on their own.
plainLanguage.businessImpact: A visitor stuck on an error they do not understand gives up halfway. A helpful hint saves the sale.
plainLanguage.howToFix: Write error messages that say what is expected, for example Enter the date as YYYY-MM-DD, rather than just Invalid.

dosLagenReference: EN 301 549 V3.2.1, WCAG 2.1 Level AA required

remediation.description: For Web pages that cause legal commitments or financial transactions, users must be able to: Reverse, Check, or Confirm.
remediation.technicalGuidance: Offer a summary page before final submission with ability to edit.

holmdigitalInsight.swedishInterpretation: Absolute requirement for e-commerce and legal decisions.
commonMistakes: Submission of binding contracts without review
holmdigitalInsight.priorityRationale: Critical to avoid serious consequences of mistakes.

legalContext.eaaAnnex: Annex I, Section I - Functional accessibility requirements

plainLanguage.headline: No safety net before you commit or pay
plainLanguage.whatHappens: For purchases, contracts, or other important decisions, there is no way to check, change, or undo before you submit something binding.
plainLanguage.whoIsAffected: All visitors, especially those who easily make mistakes by accident and need a chance to review before they confirm.
plainLanguage.businessImpact: Decisions that cannot be undone lead to wrong orders, regret, and support cases. A confirmation step cuts down on costly mistakes.
plainLanguage.howToFix: Your developer adds a summary before the final step, where the visitor can review and change.

dosLagenReference: EN 301 549 V3.2.1, WCAG 2.1 Level A required

remediation.description: Update: From WCAG 2.2 this criterion is removed/obsolete, but in WCAG 2.1/EN 301 549 it applies: IDs must be unique, elements correctly nested.
remediation.technicalGuidance: Validate HTML. Ensure id attributes are unique on the page. Close all tags correctly.

holmdigitalInsight.swedishInterpretation: Less prioritized now as modern browsers handle errors well, but duplicate IDs can still break ARIA.

legalContext.eaaAnnex: Annex I, Section I - Functional accessibility requirements

plainLanguage.headline: Messy code under the surface can confuse assistive technology
plainLanguage.whatHappens: The code behind the page has faults such as duplicate markup and tags that are not closed. Modern browsers fix a lot on their own, but assistive technology can trip over it.
plainLanguage.whoIsAffected: People using a screen reader, in the cases where the messy code makes the assistive technology read something out wrong.
plainLanguage.businessImpact: Most of the time it goes unnoticed, but at worst the screen reader reads something out wrong and the visitor is misled. Cheap hygiene to sort out.
plainLanguage.howToFix: Your developer tidies the code so every piece of markup is unique and all tags are closed correctly.

dosLagenReference: EN 301 549 V3.2.1, WCAG 2.1 Level A required

remediation.description: For all components, name and role can be programmatically determined. Values can be set programmatically.
remediation.technicalGuidance: Use native HTML elements when possible. If custom components are used, ARIA (role, aria-label, aria-valuenow) must be used correctly.

holmdigitalInsight.swedishInterpretation: This is the foundation for how screen readers work with modern web apps. Without this, the app is 'invisible' to assistive technology.

legalContext.eaaAnnex: Annex I, Section I - Functional accessibility requirements

plainLanguage.headline: Icon buttons have no name
plainLanguage.whatHappens: Buttons that are shown only as an icon, such as the shopping cart or search, have no name in the code.
plainLanguage.whoIsAffected: A screen reader announces button without saying what it does. Your customer is afraid to press it.
plainLanguage.businessImpact: If the cart button has no name, your customer does not know how to get to checkout.
plainLanguage.howToFix: Give each icon button a name in the code, for example Open shopping cart. It is not visible on screen but will be read aloud.

dosLagenReference: EN 301 549 V3.2.1, WCAG 2.1 Level AA required

remediation.description: Statusmeddelanden ska kunna presenteras för användaren utan att motta fokus (via skärmläsare).
remediation.technicalGuidance: Använd aria-live regioner (polite/assertive) eller role='status'/'alert' för meddelanden som dyker upp dynamiskt (t.ex. 'Sparat', 'Sökning klar').

holmdigitalInsight.swedishInterpretation: Important in SPAs where page load does not happen. The user must know something happened.
holmdigitalInsight.priorityRationale: Provides feedback to users without sight.

legalContext.eaaAnnex: Annex I, Section I - Functional accessibility requirements

plainLanguage.headline: Important messages do not reach everyone
plainLanguage.whatHappens: When something happens without the page reloading, for example an item added to the basket or a search finishing, it only shows on screen. The screen reader does not announce it.
plainLanguage.whoIsAffected: People using a screen reader, who cannot see the confirmation and are not told that anything actually happened.
plainLanguage.businessImpact: If the visitor is not told that the item went into the basket or that something was saved, they think it did not work and either redo it or give up.
plainLanguage.howToFix: Your developer makes sure such messages are also announced by the screen reader, not just shown on screen.

dosLagenReference: EN 301 549 V3.2.1, WCAG 2.1 Level A required

remediation.description: The page must have exactly one 'main' landmark.
remediation.technicalGuidance: Use the <main> element once per page to identify the main content. Avoid having multiple <main> without unique labels, or missing it entirely.

holmdigitalInsight.swedishInterpretation: Screen reader users rely on landmarks to navigate quickly to the content. Missing <main> makes it difficult to skip navigation.

legalContext.eaaAnnex: Annex I, Section I - Functional accessibility requirements

plainLanguage.headline: The page has no clearly signposted main area
plainLanguage.whatHappens: The page is missing a single clearly marked main content area. Screen readers use these signposts, called landmarks, to let users jump straight to the content they need.
plainLanguage.whoIsAffected: Visitors using screen readers or keyboard-only navigation, and anyone who finds it hard to skip past menus and headers to get to the content.
plainLanguage.businessImpact: Visitors who cannot navigate quickly give up and leave. A page without a main landmark costs you visitors who rely on assistive technology.
plainLanguage.howToFix: Wrap the main content of the page in a single HTML main element. Your developer can fix this in minutes.

dosLagenReference: EN 301 549 V3.2.1, WCAG 2.1 Level A required

remediation.description: The page must have a level 1 heading (<h1>).
remediation.technicalGuidance: Ensure there is exactly one <h1> describing the page's unique content.

holmdigitalInsight.swedishInterpretation: A clear <h1> is critical for users to understand where they have landed. It is often the first thing a screen reader user looks for.
commonMistakes: Using logo as the only <h1> without text

legalContext.eaaAnnex: Annex I, Section I - Functional accessibility requirements

plainLanguage.headline: The page has no clear main heading
plainLanguage.whatHappens: The page has no main heading (a so called H1) to say what the page is about. The main heading is the most important one and the first thing a screen reader looks for to sum up the page.
plainLanguage.whoIsAffected: Visitors using a screen reader who jump between headings to grasp a page quickly, and anyone skimming the page to see if they have landed in the right place.
plainLanguage.businessImpact: Without a clear main heading, the visitor cannot tell at once whether they have come to the right place. That uncertainty makes more of them leave before they finish reading, and Google also has a harder time understanding what the page is about.
plainLanguage.howToFix: Your developer adds exactly one main heading at the top of the content that describes that particular page in its own words.

dosLagenReference: EN 301 549 V3.2.1, WCAG 2.1 Level A required

remediation.description: Headings must follow a logical order (h1 -> h2 -> h3).
remediation.technicalGuidance: Do not skip heading levels (e.g. directly from h1 to h3).

holmdigitalInsight.swedishInterpretation: Incorrect heading structure makes it difficult for screen readers to navigate. Never skip levels.
commonMistakes: Using h3 for styling instead of structure

legalContext.eaaAnnex: Annex I, Section I - Functional accessibility requirements

plainLanguage.headline: Headings do not follow a logical order
plainLanguage.whatHappens: The headings on the page do not follow a logical sequence in the code, so the page structure cannot be read.
plainLanguage.whoIsAffected: Screen reader users navigate via headings, much like a table of contents. Without a clear order it becomes confusing.
plainLanguage.businessImpact: A hard-to-navigate page means your visitor cannot find what they came for and leaves.
plainLanguage.howToFix: Build headings in order, with one main heading and sub-headings beneath it, just like in a document.

dosLagenReference: EN 301 549 V3.2.1, WCAG 2.1 Level A required

remediation.description: The banner (<header>) must be at the top level.
remediation.technicalGuidance: Do not place <header> inside another landmark if it is the page's main banner.

holmdigitalInsight.swedishInterpretation: The page's main menu/banner must be located correctly in the structure to be found quickly.

legalContext.eaaAnnex: Annex I, Section I - Functional accessibility requirements

plainLanguage.headline: The page header sits in the wrong place in the structure
plainLanguage.whatHappens: The page header is wrapped in the wrong place in the code instead of sitting at the top as its own region. Assistive technology then does not find it as easily.
plainLanguage.whoIsAffected: People using a screen reader who tend to jump straight to the header to reach the logo, menu, and search.
plainLanguage.businessImpact: A small structural slip that makes navigation a little more awkward for assistive technology users. Worth fixing, but marginal.
plainLanguage.howToFix: Your developer moves the header so it sits at the top as its own region, not inside something else.

dosLagenReference: EN 301 549 V3.2.1, WCAG 2.1 Level A required

remediation.description: The page must have only one 'banner' landmark (usually <header>).
remediation.technicalGuidance: Ensure you only have one <header> at the top level.

holmdigitalInsight.swedishInterpretation: Multiple banners confuse navigation. There should be only one top header.
commonMistakes: Having header both at top and bottom

legalContext.eaaAnnex: Annex I, Section I - Functional accessibility requirements

plainLanguage.headline: The page has more than one header
plainLanguage.whatHappens: The page is marked up with more than one header. Assistive technology expects a single one and is confused by several.
plainLanguage.whoIsAffected: People using a screen reader who navigate by the page's regions and cannot tell which header is the right one.
plainLanguage.businessImpact: Duplicate headers make navigation unclear for assistive technology users, but it is a small thing to tidy away.
plainLanguage.howToFix: Your developer makes sure only the top part is marked up as the header.

dosLagenReference: EN 301 549 V3.2.1, WCAG 2.1 Level A required

remediation.description: Landmarks must have unique roles or labels.
remediation.technicalGuidance: If you have multiple <nav> elements, give them unique 'aria-label' (e.g., 'Main Menu', 'Footer Menu').

holmdigitalInsight.swedishInterpretation: The user must be able to distinguish between different menus/regions. Give them names.

legalContext.eaaAnnex: Annex I, Section I - Functional accessibility requirements

plainLanguage.headline: Several regions on the page share the same name
plainLanguage.whatHappens: The page has several identical regions, for example several menus, without giving them their own names. Assistive technology cannot tell them apart.
plainLanguage.whoIsAffected: People using a screen reader who list the page's regions and see several with the same name without knowing which is which.
plainLanguage.businessImpact: Identical regions with no names make navigating with assistive technology harder, but it is a minor adjustment.
plainLanguage.howToFix: Your developer gives each region its own name, for example Main menu and Footer menu.

dosLagenReference: EN 301 549 V3.2.1, WCAG 2.1 Level A required

remediation.description: All content on the page must be contained within landmarks (regions).
remediation.technicalGuidance: Ensure all content is inside <main>, <header>, <nav>, <footer>, or <aside>.

holmdigitalInsight.swedishInterpretation: For screen reader users to navigate effectively, the page must be divided into logical regions.

legalContext.eaaAnnex: Annex I, Section I - Functional accessibility requirements

plainLanguage.headline: Page content is not organised into signposted areas
plainLanguage.whatHappens: Parts of the page sit outside any signposted area. Screen readers divide a page into named regions such as header, navigation, main content, and footer, so users can jump directly to what they need.
plainLanguage.whoIsAffected: Visitors using screen readers, keyboard navigation, or other assistive tools that rely on page structure to move around efficiently.
plainLanguage.businessImpact: When the page has no clear structure, screen reader users cannot skip straight to the main content. They navigate line by line and give up before completing their task.
plainLanguage.howToFix: Wrap all content in appropriate HTML elements such as header, nav, main, and footer. Your developer can restructure the page layout to meet this requirement.

dosLagenReference: WCAG 2.2 criterion (Level AA), not yet a legal requirement. The legal floor is WCAG 2.1 Level AA via EN 301 549 V3.2.1 (referenced in the Official Journal of the EU). It becomes applicable once EN 301 549 V4.x is referenced in the OJEU.

remediation.description: Interactive targets (buttons, links, icons, form controls) must be at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, or have at least 24 pixels of clear spacing to the nearest other target. Exceptions apply to links in flowing text, to controls whose size is determined by the browser, and where an equivalent control of sufficient size exists on the same page.
remediation.technicalGuidance: Give interactive elements at least a 24px hit area, ideally via min-height and min-width on the control itself. If the icon must look small, keep the small icon but enlarge the hit area with padding, or leave at least 24px of clearance around it (the spacing exception). Measure the actual hit area, not the visual size of the icon.

holmdigitalInsight.swedishInterpretation: This is the only one of the new 2.2 criteria that our scanner actually detects automatically, so it is often the first time a client sees "WCAG 2.2" in a report. Interpret it in practice like this: count the actual hit area, not the visual size of the icon. A bin icon that looks 16 pixels wide may have an invisible 24-pixel hit area around it, in which case the criterion is met. Conversely, a large button with a small real hit area fails. In practice it most often trips on dense toolbars, close icons in modals, social icons in the footer, and pagination. Note that this is not yet a legal requirement in Sweden (the legal floor is WCAG 2.1 AA), but it is cheap to fix and hits mobile use directly, so we recommend it anyway. The spacing exception (24 pixels of clearance) often saves small icons without making them visually larger.
commonMistakes: Icon buttons (close icons, hamburger menus, share icons) with a hit area below 24 pixels
Pagination numbers and breadcrumbs spaced too tightly without 24 pixels of clearance between them
Small toggles and checkboxes in forms, especially in compact tables
Links stacked on top of each other in footers and menus without enough line spacing
holmdigitalInsight.priorityRationale: High value for the cost. Primarily affects mobile and touch users, people with motor or tremor conditions, and anyone using a screen at arm's length. Not yet a legal requirement under DOS-lagen (the floor is still WCAG 2.1 AA), but cheap to fix and the only WCAG 2.2 criterion the scanner detects automatically, so it carries outsized signalling value in a report.

plainLanguage.headline: Buttons and icons are too small to tap
plainLanguage.whatHappens: Some buttons, links and icons have a tap area that is too small. They are hard to hit with a finger on a touch screen.
plainLanguage.whoIsAffected: People with hand tremors or reduced fine motor control, many older users, and anyone using a phone on the move.
plainLanguage.businessImpact: When a visitor misses the button and taps the wrong thing, they often give up instead of trying again. Small tap targets cost you conversions, especially on mobile where most of your visitors are.
plainLanguage.howToFix: Make the tap area at least the size of a fingertip, or add space around small icons so they do not sit on top of each other. We point out exactly which ones are too small.

dosLagenReference: WCAG 2.2 criterion (Level AA), not yet a legal requirement. The legal floor is WCAG 2.1 Level AA via EN 301 549 V3.2.1 (referenced in the Official Journal of the EU). It becomes applicable once EN 301 549 V4.x is referenced in the OJEU.

remediation.description: Anything that can be done with a dragging movement must also be operable with a single pointer action (such as a single click or tap), unless the dragging movement is essential to the function or is determined by the underlying technology. A slider that is dragged must therefore also be operable with clickable plus and minus buttons or by clicking a position on the track.
remediation.technicalGuidance: Provide a clickable alternative for every drag gesture: plus and minus buttons on sliders, arrows on carousels, up and down buttons on sortable lists, zoom and position buttons on maps. Listen for click and pointerup events on discrete controls, not just pointermove. Keyboard support alone is not enough; the criterion concerns pointer use without dragging.

holmdigitalInsight.swedishInterpretation: This is about never locking a function behind dragging alone. Interpret it broadly: maps that only pan by dragging, price sliders and image comparators that only work by dragging, reorderable lists where you have to drag rows, and carousels that only respond to swiping. For each such pattern there must be a clickable alternative that does the same thing. Drag that moves freely in two directions (drawing, drag-and-drop to any position) is often essential and then the exception applies, but most drag on an ordinary website is really a choice between a few states and works perfectly well as a click instead. Not yet a legal requirement in Sweden, but one of the more invisible barriers: it does not show up in an automated scan and quietly affects those who cannot drag precisely.
commonMistakes: Maps and image comparators that can only be panned or dragged, with no clickable controls
Price sliders without plus and minus buttons or a clickable track
Sortable lists (drag to reorder) without up and down buttons as an alternative
Carousels and slideshows that only respond to swiping, with no visible arrows
holmdigitalInsight.priorityRationale: Affects people who cannot perform precise drag gestures: users with tremor, limited dexterity, or those navigating by keyboard, switch or head pointer. Invisible in automated scans, so it is easy to miss and easy to ship. Not yet a legal requirement under DOS-lagen, but a genuine usability barrier with usually low remediation cost.

plainLanguage.headline: Some things can only be controlled by dragging
plainLanguage.whatHappens: Some functions only work if you drag with your finger or the mouse, for example a map, a slider, or a slideshow. There is no way to click instead.
plainLanguage.whoIsAffected: People with shaky hands or reduced fine motor control, and those who use a keyboard or other assistive technology and cannot drag precisely.
plainLanguage.businessImpact: Lock a function behind a drag and you shut out everyone who cannot drag from that function.
plainLanguage.howToFix: Your developer adds clickable alternatives, for example plus and minus buttons on sliders and arrows on slideshows.

dosLagenReference: WCAG 2.2 criterion (Level AA), not yet a legal requirement. The legal floor is WCAG 2.1 Level AA via EN 301 549 V3.2.1 (referenced in the Official Journal of the EU). It becomes applicable once EN 301 549 V4.x is referenced in the OJEU.

remediation.description: When an element receives keyboard focus, it must not be entirely hidden by other content on the page, such as a sticky header, a cookie banner, a chat widget or a floating toolbar. At least part of the focused element must remain visible. (The stronger requirement that the whole element be visible is 2.4.12, which is AAA and not part of Phase 1.)
remediation.technicalGuidance: Set scroll-margin-top on focusable elements so they do not end up behind a sticky header when the page scrolls focus into view. Account for the height of sticky elements and floating UI when calculating the visible area. Avoid permanent overlays (cookie banners, chat bubbles) that cover focused content; give them a lower z-index than the focus ring or move them out of the focus flow.

holmdigitalInsight.swedishInterpretation: This is a criterion you only find by actually tabbing through the page. Interpret it practically: the most common cause is a sticky header that follows along as you scroll. When focus tabs downward and the page scrolls up, the focused element can end up behind the header and become entirely invisible. The keyboard user then has no idea where they are. The same happens behind cookie banners, persistent chat bubbles and floating buttons in the corner. The minimum bar is low: it is enough that some part of the element is visible, it need not be fully clear. In practice it is usually solved with scroll-margin-top on focusable elements or by giving the sticky element the right height allowance. Not yet a legal requirement in Sweden, but cheap to fix and immediately felt by anyone navigating with a keyboard.
commonMistakes: Sticky header that covers the element that has just received focus during scrolling
Cookie banner or consent dialog that covers focused content at the top of the page
Persistent chat bubble or support button in the corner that hides focus behind it
Missing scroll-margin so that focus lands at the edge of or behind a fixed element
holmdigitalInsight.priorityRationale: Affects keyboard and screen-magnifier users who lose track of focus when it disappears behind sticky or floating UI. Cannot be caught by an automated scan; only tab-through testing reveals it. Not yet a legal requirement under DOS-lagen, but low-cost to fix (often a single CSS property) and a real orientation barrier.

plainLanguage.headline: Visitors lose track of where they are on the page
plainLanguage.whatHappens: When you move through the page with the keyboard, the thing you just selected can end up behind a header that stays at the top, a cookie box, or a chat bubble. Then you can no longer see where you are.
plainLanguage.whoIsAffected: People who navigate by keyboard and people who magnify the screen, and who lose their bearings when the highlight disappears behind something.
plainLanguage.businessImpact: A visitor who cannot see where they are on the page becomes uneasy and quits. It is felt most in forms and the checkout.
plainLanguage.howToFix: Your developer makes sure the selected item is always visible, by leaving room so it does not end up behind fixed elements.
